front_blocks.md: What are **halogenoalkanes**?

back_blocks.md: **Halogenoalkanes** are organic compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms in an alkane have been replaced by a halogen atom (F, Cl, Br or I).
They are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary depending on the carbon bearing the halogen.

front_blocks.md: Define **primary halogenoalkane**

back_blocks.md: A **primary halogenoalkane** is one in which the halogen is attached to a carbon that is bonded to only one other alkyl group.
For example, 1-bromopropane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br) is a primary halogenoalkane.

front_blocks.md: Define **secondary halogenoalkane**

One alkyl group = primary. Two alkyl groups = secondary. Three alkyl groups = tertiary.

front_blocks.md: Why do **aqueous** NaOH and **ethanolic** NaOH give different products when reacting with a halogenoalkane?

back_blocks.md: Aqueous NaOH causes **nucleophilic substitution**, producing an alcohol.
Ethanolic NaOH causes **elimination**, producing an alkene because the solvent favours the elimination pathway.

front_blocks.md: Define **nucleophilic substitution**

back_blocks.md: A **nucleophilic substitution** is a reaction in which a nucleophile attacks a carbon atom carrying a partial positive charge and replaces an atom or group carrying a partial negative charge.

front_blocks.md: Why do **halogenoalkanes** undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions?

back_blocks.md: The **C-X bond is polar** because of the large difference in electronegativity between carbon and the halogen.
This gives the carbon atom a partial positive charge (δ+), making it susceptible to attack by a nucleophile.

front_blocks.md: Describe the mechanism of nucleophilic substitution when bromoethane reacts with aqueous OH<sup>-</sup>.

back_blocks.md: The OH<sup>-</sup> ion donates a lone pair to the **δ+ carbon** of the C-Br bond, forming a new C-O bond.
Simultaneously, the C-Br bond breaks heterolytically and the bromide ion (Br<sup>-</sup>) is expelled as a leaving group, producing ethanol.

front_blocks.md: Describe the **two steps** in the reaction of chloromethane with excess ammonia to form methylamine.

back_blocks.md: Step 1: NH<sub>3</sub> attacks the **δ+ carbon** of CH<sub>3</sub>Cl by **nucleophilic substitution**, forming [CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup>.

Step 2: A second NH<sub>3</sub> molecule acts as a **base**, removing a proton from [CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup> to give methylamine (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup>.

front_blocks.md: Describe the experimental method used to **compare the rate of hydrolysis** of different halogenoalkanes.

back_blocks.md: Three test tubes are set up in a **50°C water bath**, each containing ethanol and **acidified silver nitrate** solution.
A few drops of a chloroalkane, bromoalkane and iodoalkane are added to separate test tubes and a stopwatch is started. The time for each **precipitate** to form is recorded.

front_blocks.md: Why is **no precipitate** formed when a fluoroalkane is used in the silver nitrate hydrolysis test?

back_blocks.md: Silver fluoride is **soluble**, so no precipitate forms even if fluoride ions are produced.
This also confirms that fluoroalkanes are the least reactive halogenoalkanes and do not undergo significant hydrolysis.

front_blocks.md: Define **bond enthalpy**

back_blocks.md: **Bond enthalpy** is the energy required to break one mole of a covalent bond in the gaseous state, averaged across similar chemical environments.
A higher bond enthalpy means the bond is stronger and harder to break.

front_blocks.md: State the order of **C-X bond enthalpies** from weakest to strongest across the halogenoalkanes.

back_blocks.md: C-I < C-Br < C-Cl < C-F.
The **C-I bond** is the weakest and easiest to break, making **iodoalkanes** the most reactive. The C-F bond is the strongest, making fluoroalkanes the least reactive.

front_blocks.md: Why do different halogenoalkanes have **different rates** of substitution reactions?

back_blocks.md: The rate depends on the **bond enthalpy** of the C-X bond.
Weaker C-X bonds (lower bond enthalpy) break more easily, allowing the nucleophile to replace the halogen faster. The C-I bond is weakest, so iodoalkanes react fastest.
